opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when the opportunities started coming in, I tried not to be swayed by the headline numbers, whether that's the valuation, the funding round, or the title they were offering. In this environment a lot of teams can raise money quickly, so money alone doesn't tell you much.

The first thing I looked at was the problem itself. Is this team working on something fundamental, something I'd find intellectually exciting for years, or is it a thin layer on top of someone else's model? I've spent a long time on research, from reinforcement learning to planning and reasoning to the efficiency of large models, and I wanted a place where that research could directly shape the product rather than being a side project.

The second thing was the people. In a small team the founders really define the culture. I asked myself: do they understand what research actually takes? Are they willing to tolerate the uncertainty, the experiments that fail, the months where nothing seems to work? Some teams want a "chief scientist" mostly as a signal to investors. That's not a role I'm interested in. I'd rather be hands-on, writing code, running experiments, and mentoring people.

Third, I thought about autonomy and direction. At a big company you have huge resources, but priorities can shift for reasons that have nothing to do with the science. At a startup you have more freedom, but fewer GPUs and much more pressure to show results. So I wanted to understand concretely how much compute they had, how they planned to allocate it, and whether their roadmap left room for longer-term bets.

Finally, I asked a simpler, more personal question: if this company failed in three years, would I still feel the time was well spent? Would I have learned something, built something meaningful, and worked with people I respect? If the answer was yes, the role was worth seriously considering. If it only made sense in the scenario where everything goes perfectly, I was much more cautious.

r001.rationale: The response says he preferred hands-on work and was wary of a chief scientist role used as an investor signal, but it does not state that he preferred being a co-founder over joining as a hired AI or research head.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when those offers started coming in, I tried not to think about them as job offers in the usual sense, like comparing salary or title. I asked myself three questions.

The first was about the problem itself. Is this a question I would be thinking about anyway, even if nobody paid me? I spent a long time at Meta working on things like search, reasoning, and training dynamics, and I know I do my best work when I'm genuinely curious. If a team's core problem didn't make me want to open a notebook that evening, I treated that as a signal, no matter how good the terms looked.

The second was about the people. In a startup you're not joining a research org with a thousand colleagues to buffer you. You're joining maybe five or ten people, and you'll be in a room with them every day under a lot of pressure. So I spent time talking to the founders, not about the pitch deck but about how they argue, how they handle being wrong, what they do when an experiment fails. You learn a lot more from how someone reacts to a disagreement than from their vision statement.

The third was whether the role actually gave me room to matter. Some teams really just wanted a well-known name to put on the website or to help with fundraising. That's flattering for about a week. I wanted a place where the technical direction was still open, where the decisions I make in the first year would shape what the company becomes.

And I'll admit there was a less rational factor too. At a big company, you're one input among many. At a startup, you feel the consequences of your own judgment very directly. That's frightening, but after many years it's also what I wanted. So in the end I didn't pick the safest offer or the richest one. I picked the one where, if it failed, I would still feel the time was well spent.

r001.rationale: The response describes evaluating problem fit, founders, and influence over technical direction, but never says Tian preferred being a co-founder over taking a hired AI or research leadership role.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key question was what I would actually get to do. Would I be able to work on the technical problems I cared about and have enough influence to shape the direction? A title alone doesn’t tell you that.

I’d also look at how the team’s strengths complemented mine. What would I bring that they were missing, and what could they do that I couldn’t do on my own? Then there’s alignment with the founders—whether we agree on what to build and how to balance research with getting a product out. Those things would matter more to me than how impressive the role sounded.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the work, influence, team fit, and founder alignment he would value, but never says he preferred being a co-founder over taking a hired head of AI or research role.
